attacks.claim: The up migration is not a rename. It adds an empty private_notes column and drops notes without copying any data, so every existing user note is destroyed when the migration auto-runs on deploy. The PR's 'pure rename, no data change' claim is false, and the notes are unrecoverable elsewhere.
attacks.evidence: ALTER TABLE user_recipes ADD COLUMN private_notes text; ALTER TABLE user_recipes DROP COLUMN notes;

attacks.claim: The down migration cannot restore data. It re-adds notes as NULL and drops private_notes, so any rollback after the up migration permanently loses all note text written before and after the change.
attacks.evidence: ALTER TABLE user_recipes ADD COLUMN notes text; ALTER TABLE user_recipes DROP COLUMN private_notes;

attacks.claim: Migrations auto-run on deploy with no backup, snapshot, or pre-migration checkpoint, and the change is irreversible. Nothing protects the 140M-row table before the destructive DROP.
attacks.evidence: Migrations run automatically on deploy after merge to main. ... the down migration restores the old name.

attacks.claim: DROP COLUMN notes runs in the same deploy as the new code with no expand/contract sequencing. Old instances still selecting ur.notes fail during the rolling deploy, and rolling back app code after the migration also breaks the endpoint.

The handler loads every saved row for the user (up to 200k+, joined to recipes, including notes text) on every request and slices one page in memory. This is unbounded work per request and will not fit the 300ms p99 budget.
attacks.evidence: const { rows } = await db.query<SavedRow>(` ... `WHERE ur.user_id = $1` ... `ORDER BY ur.saved_at DESC, ur.id DESC`, `[userId],` ... `const page = rows.slice(start, start + limit);`

attacks.claim: The cursor is resolved by a linear findIndex over the full result, with no keyset predicate, so the database cannot seek to the cursor. Each page costs O(n).
attacks.evidence: const start = cursor ? rows.findIndex((r) => r.id === cursor) + 1 : 0;

attacks.claim: No index supports the (user_id, saved_at DESC, id DESC) sort or filter, and the migration adds none. Each request sorts up to 200k rows per user on a 140M-row table.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no CREATE INDEX on user_recipes(user_id, saved_at DESC, id DESC) in 0087_private_notes.up.sql or the PR.

attacks.claim: DROP COLUMN takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the 140M-row table with no lock_timeout, so it can queue behind a long-running query and then block all reads and writes on user_recipes.
attacks.evidence: BEGIN; ALTER TABLE user_recipes ADD COLUMN private_notes text; ALTER TABLE user_recipes DROP COLUMN notes; COMMIT; (no SET lock_timeout)

attacks.claim: An unknown or stale cursor (for example, the item was unsaved between pages) makes findIndex return -1, so start becomes 0. The client silently gets page one again and can loop forever or duplicate items instead of receiving an error.
attacks.evidence: const start = cursor ? rows.findIndex((r) => r.id === cursor) + 1 : 0;

attacks.claim: A non-positive limit is not clamped below. Math.min does not stop negatives, so limit=-1 yields an empty page, nextCursor is computed as non-null, and page[page.length - 1] is undefined, which throws and returns a 500.
attacks.evidence: const limit = Math.min(Number(req.query.limit) || 50, 100); ... start + limit < rows.length ? page[page.length - 1].id : null;

attacks.claim: Removing offset is a silent breaking change. Clients still sending offset get the first page on every request, with no error, versioning, or deprecation signal.

The response now returns private_notes from a user-scoped endpoint. The PR's stated rationale is that this field must never reach shared views, so the PR should confirm this route is never reachable from a shared or public surface.
attacks.evidence: SELECT ur.id, ur.recipe_id, r.title, ur.saved_at, ur.private_notes
